extraction_notes: Extracted from the 2026-27 Program of Studies PDF (44 pages; page 1 is the cover). The 2025-26 HTML copy in catalogs/ was not used (older, and the 2026-27 catalog covers all courses). Course headers give '1 Block/credit' etc.; credits taken from these as printed. Length is 'unknown' unless the catalog states semester/year (Band, Choir, Calculus, Driver Education). Humanities appears under both English and Social Studies; one record. Language Levels I-V (German and Spanish) are split into one record per language with the shared description. Mount Abraham UHS courses and Hannaford Career Center (PAHCC) programs are mentioned but no course/program names are listed (Mount Abe: 'Detailed course descriptions will be provided during the course registration process'), so no records were made; online (VTVLC) courses likewise have no named courses. Flexible pathway programs with descriptions (Dual Enrollment, Early College, Middlebury College, Walden Year) are recorded as programs with department 'Flexible Pathways Options'. Pre-Calculus description in the source contains a stray duplicated lead-in sentence, copied as printed. The catalog's department introductions (e.g. Driver Education pass/fail note) are not course descriptions and are only summarized in notes where relevant.

graduation_requirements.raw_text:
Each Vergennes Union High School graduate will meet graduation requirements through a minimum
of 22.5 credits, earned through approved courses and or equivalent learning experiences via Flexible
Pathways. These pathways may include independent studies, online courses, Career and Technical
Center programs, internships, dual enrollment, and early college.
Successful completion of a course at VUHS indicates that a student has earned proficiency credit for
that course. Proficiency credit is awarded based on established grading criteria and is further
explained in the Grade Reporting section of this document.
Credit Requirements for Graduation (Minimum of 22.5 credits)
4 credits in English
3 credits in Mathematics
3 credits in Science
3 credits in Social Studies
1 credit in US History and .5 credit in Civics
US History meets the US History requirement
Modern Citizenship or Advanced Placement Government and Politics meets the Civics requirement
1 credit in Visual or Performing Arts
1.5 credits in Physical Education
.5 credit in Health
.5 credit in Technology
.5 credit in Financial Literacy
Personal Finance meets this requirement
5.5 credits in Electives
For students who are eligible for alternate pathways to graduation, such as an Individualized Education Plan or a Multi Year Plan, please
refer to the Student and Family Handbook or your case manager for more information.

courses.description: The primary intensive project undertaken by the class is raising a flock of chickens. Students learn about animal anatomy and physiology, animal nutrition, and the care required for farm animals. They study animal health and perform a basic physical examination on a dairy cow. The course includes field trips to evaluate various soil sites for their agricultural potential. Students also learn greenhouse plant propagation techniques and participate in field trips to local agricultural operations. Additionally, they research current animal ethics issues. This course serves as an introduction to agricultural science, preparing students for further studies in Sustainable Agriculture or Natural Resource Management at the Hannaford Career Center.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is eligible to earn .5 Science credit and .5 elective credit, or 1.0 elective credit. Please consult your school counselor for details.
courses.notes: Agricultural Science dept: courses satisfy elective requirements, with the option of technology and science credits

courses.description: In this pre-technical course, students learn how to safely operate tractors and can earn a tractor safety certification. The class focuses on understanding how small engines work and how to fix them. Students gain skills in engine maintenance and troubleshooting, along with learning repair techniques and maintenance strategies. This course is a great starting point for students who want to pursue programs in Automotive, Diesel, Sustainable Agriculture, or Natural Resources Management at the Hannaford Career Center.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is eligible to earn .5 Science credit and .5 elective credit, or 1.0 elective credit. Please consult your school counselor for details.
courses.notes: Agricultural Science dept: courses satisfy elective requirements, with the option of technology and science credits

courses.description: This pre-technical course helps students learn important skills in various trades, including metal fabrication, electrical wiring, plumbing, surveying, and carpentry. Students explore different welding techniques, such as shielded metal arc welding (stick), gas metal arc welding (wire feed), and plasma arc cutting. There is plenty of hands-on practice, where students design and complete projects.The course also covers the basics of electrical wiring, including direct current and alternating current. Students design, build, and test simple circuits. Additionally, they practice carpentry by creating wooden structures. This course lays the groundwork for students who are interested in pursuing programs in Welding, Construction, or Manufacturing at the Hannaford Career Center.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is eligible to earn .5 Science credit. Please consult your school counselor for details.
courses.notes: Agricultural Science dept: courses satisfy elective requirements, with the option of technology and science credits

courses.description: Driver Education equips students with the skills and knowledge needed to drive safely and responsibly. This course addresses essential questions such as how driving decisions impact personal and community wellness, how to prevent accidents, and how self-awareness affects driving behavior. Key Focus Areas: ●Developing safe driving habits and decision-making skills to reduce accident risks. ●Addressing critical issues like DUI, distractions, and sleep deprivation. ●Preparing students for the Vermont Driver’s Exam through classroom and behind-the-wheel instruction. Course Requirements: ●Classroom Instruction: 30 hours ●Behind-the-Wheel Instruction: 6 hours with a licensed instructor and 40 hours supervised driving with an adult. Outcomes: ●Students who meet academic and driving standards will earn a certificate to test for their license. Those who do not complete requirements may retake the course or arrange additional practice time. ●Parental involvement and supervised practice are strongly encouraged to ensure student success and safety on the road.
courses.prerequisites: Students must be 15 years of age and hold a valid learner’s permit BEFORE the class begins.
courses.notes: Department note: graded on a pass/fail basis; students are assigned to the first or second semester in order of their birthdate.

courses.description: Community-Based Learning (CBL) is a hands-on course for students who want to learn by doing and make meaningful connections beyond the classroom. In CBL, students explore personal interests and career pathways by working with community partners such as schools, nonprofits, government offices, businesses, and organizations. Students will develop goals connected to their interests and apply academic, workplace, and life skills in real-world settings. Through regular reflection, students build skills such as responsibility, communication, problem-solving, and self-direction, while gaining a deeper understanding of their community and potential future paths. CBL is best suited for students who are motivated, independent, and interested in learning through real-world experiences. The course is graded on a pass/fail basis and includes time spent at a community placement along with guided reflection and goal-setting supported by the CBL teacher.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Expanded Learning Opportunities (ELO) allows students to design a personalized learning experience based on their interests, goals, or career exploration. Students may create their own course, develop an in-depth project, or work with a community organization or business. Examples include studying a specialized topic like astronomy or World War II, completing a hands-on project such as farm work or safety initiatives, or partnering with local organizations like museums or environmental groups. Students work with an educator to plan, carry out, and reflect on their learning. This course is best suited for students who are self-directed, motivated, and interested in learning beyond a traditional classroom setting.
courses.credits_text: Expanded Learning Opportunities                           .5 Block/credit or 1 Block/credit
courses.notes: program; Credit is .5 or 1; credits field holds the minimum

courses.description: This course focuses on four major areas: 1) budgeting and financial planning for your financial goals; 2) investing and risk mitigation; 3) our tax system; and 4) credit, loans and building for a financially successful future. You will explore how your education and career choice affect your financial future. This course will help you develop specific tools and a financial sense of your future as a member of the workforce, as a responsible citizen, and as an effective participant in a global economy.
courses.fulfills_text: Students must show evidence of proficiency in the area of financial literacy in order to meet graduation requirements.

courses.description: This course provides time for students to pursue a personal interest in depth. With support from the instructor, students design their own learning experience, set their own goals, and create their own unique ways to demonstrate what they have learned. Students are free to explore any topic or project of their choice, whether an academic subject, a practical skill, a career interest, a leadership experience, an artistic creation, or an engineering design. Students can even earn credit for learning linked to extracurricular activities such as student council and yearbook, or an after-school job. Projects can take place in or out of school; final products can range from traditional presentations or written pieces to multimedia creations to exhibits, events, or physical objects.
courses.notes: program; Credit is .5 or 1; credits field holds the minimum

courses.course_name: STRIVE - Strategies To Reinforce Individualized Visions of Education
courses.description: STRIVE is available by recommendation for students in grades 9-12. The foundation of this course is to reflect and build on students’ knowledge and understanding of the guideline “I challenge myself”, and understand through self-challenge that I can grow as a learner. Students are taught learning strategies, which will help them become more active, independent learners. STRIVE is designed to investigate, identify and further understand oneself as a learner in all environments. In addition to learning strategies, students have opportunities to work on goals in basic academic skills. These are different for every student, depending on needs, and might include reading comprehension, math computation, or writing. Students have opportunities to apply learning strategies and academic skills while receiving support with coursework or while preparing for tests.
courses.notes: Available by recommendation

courses.description: Skills in Literature is a highly individualized course designed to develop your basic literacy skills through the exploration of various types and samples of literature from around the world. The course offers a chance for you to work closely with a teacher in a smaller group setting, helping you identify and reach your writing and reading goals.

In this course, you will examine a wide variety of literature and non-fiction texts, with emphasis on building reading and writing skills essential for high school success. You will be introduced to the close reading of texts and develop an understanding of writing as a process. Writing instruction focuses on clarity, development of ideas, and literary techniques, as well as on sentence crafting and parts of speech.
courses.notes: Foundational course that supports access to future coursework, recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

courses.description: This course explores the foundations of the American experience through study of the stories we tell about ourselves and complements the tenth grade US History course. You’ll examine important ideas such as tolerance, rebellion, individualism, and community by reading and discussing novels, short stories, plays, essays, and political documents. In American Literature, you’ll create personal written responses to literary and informational texts using pre-writing, outlining, drafting, revising, proofreading, and presenting texts as part of a literate community.
courses.prerequisites: 9th Grade English
courses.notes: Foundational course that supports access to future coursework, recommended for 10th graders (will be preselected for 10th grade students)

courses.description: This course emphasizes student choice for reading and writing, allowing both advanced and inexperienced students to grow at their own pace. Adventure stories, science fiction, travel journals, classic novels, non-fiction, biographies, poetry . . . the library is yours to explore. Working alone or in small groups, you will choose what to read and what sort of projects or presentations will demonstrate your learning. Written work will also be flexible. Some students focus on traditional essays. Others write short stories or poems. Others polish college application essays or job-related writing, such as resumes. Classwork consists of time for reading and writing, discussions, mini-lessons, teacher conferencing, and presentations to the class. Recommended for students at any level interested in exploring new worlds, expanding their reading, and continuing to improve their writing skills. *This can be a dual enrollment course opportunity through Community College of Vermont if it meets CCV’s enrollment criteria. 10th grade students may take this course concurrently with American Literature.
courses.prerequisites: 9th Grade English
courses.notes: Footnote *: can be a dual enrollment opportunity through Community College of Vermont if it meets CCV's enrollment criteria

courses.description: In this course you will follow the history of English language, literature, and culture, exploring timeless themes such as heroic quests, the struggle of good versus evil, the problems of faith and doubt, the attractions of love and beauty, and the corruption of power. You will practice in-depth analysis of classic stories and respond to these tales through interpretive essays, argument, and personal narratives. Recommended for students interested in the history of literature, in college-level reading skills, and in discussion of important ideas.
courses.prerequisites: 9th Grade English & American Literature

courses.description: In this class you will be introduced to “reading” images and visual texts, such as film, television, still photos, and computer multimedia sources. You will learn the terminology and concepts of visual text analysis, evaluate visual communication including media bias, and practice interpreting a wide variety of specific visual texts. You will respond to visual texts through writing and storyboarding, as well as creating visual texts. Recommended for students interested in study of film and other media.
courses.prerequisites: 9th Grade English & American Literature

courses.description: In this course, you will study literary “voice” through both reading and writing. Close reading activities will teach you to discover meaning in a wide variety of texts (fiction and nonfiction, written and visual). Formal and informal writing assignments help you refine your personal writing process and create texts of your own, including dramatic performances, film storyboards, analytical essays, and various creative writing pieces. This course includes the study of novels, plays, poetry, short stories, essays, drama, film, and television. Recommended for all students.
courses.prerequisites: 9th Grade English & American Literature

courses.description: In this interdisciplinary honors course you will address some of the core questions of human existence: What is the purpose of life? How should I live? What should I value? How should I relate to others and to the world? How do I know what is true, what is good, what is beautiful? Students explore these questions by examining the art, literature, and philosophy of diverse cultures throughout history. The focus is on the relationships between self, society, and subject matter. The purpose is not to teach specific answers, but to help you develop, clarify, and enrich your own belief systems and to deepen your understanding of yourself. The course concludes with student presentations of extended personal research essays to a panel of community members. Recommended for students interested in engaging deeply with important ideas and personal beliefs.
courses.prerequisites: 9th Grade English & American Literature
courses.notes: Also listed under Social Studies (page 36) with the same grades, credit and a near-identical description; recorded once

courses.description: AP Language and Composition emphasizes the expository, analytical, and argumentative writing that forms the basis of academic and professional communication, as well as the personal and reflective writing that fosters development of writing in context. Close reading and rhetorical analysis of various non-fiction essays, articles, and books guide you toward deeper understandings of complex texts and prepare you to write prose of sufficient richness to communicate effectively with mature readers. This course is writing and reading intensive and offers you the opportunity to earn college credit through the College Board’s AP exam in May. Recommended for students who are well organized and highly motivated to study language, rhetoric, and non-fiction writing in depth.
courses.prerequisites: English teacher signature on course selection sheet. Successful completion of summer reading assignments and acceptable performance on the assessment of summer reading assignments.

courses.description: In this course students challenge themselves physically and mentally in an atmosphere that is safe, supportive, and fun. The program is designed to build confidence, self-esteem, trust, cooperation, and communication skills. Activities may include, but are not limited to, noncompetitive games, group problem solving initiatives, trust activities, knot tying, belaying techniques, as well as low and high ropes course challenges.
courses.notes: Recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

courses.description: This class is a skills based learning environment focusing on varying dimensions of wellness. Some examples of skills practiced include, but are not limited to, analyzing influences, advocacy, decision making and accessing valid and reliable information. The class covers topics including mental health/mental illness, nutrition, substance abuse prevention, sexuality and more through projects, guest speakers and small and large group discussions.
courses.notes: Recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

courses.description: For those students who have encountered wellness and/or fitness challenges, this class is designed for you. Healthy Living & Fitness allows students to design and carry out their own personal wellness plan. Each student develops lifelong wellness skills and habits by practicing new learning in the areas of nutrition, cooking, stress management, and physical fitness. Students have help figuring out the best and easiest ways to develop core strength, tone muscles, eat nutritionally, and generally achieve physical and mental fitness.

Personal Fitness introduces students to the benefits of lifelong fitness by teaching them how to assess their fitness levels, write a personal fitness plan, and monitor and adjust the plan accordingly. Students learn proper technique and safety concerns of all weight room equipment. They are introduced to basic anatomy, the components of fitness and exercise, goal setting, and circuit training as well as examining recent trends in personal fitness.

This class combines a mixture of traditional team sports, individual sports, and lifetime leisure activities. Students demonstrate knowledge of rules and skills required to play a variety of sports. Sportsmanship, team play and fitness are incorporated into each unit. The goal is for students to learn the fundamentals skills needed for enjoyment and active participation in lifetime activities.

This class will build on the skills that students learned in PE1, and new sports and activities will be offered. Students will continue to demonstrate knowledge of rules and skills required to play while learning advanced strategies and tactics. Students will take ownership of the class through running tournaments and self-refereeing, taking responsibility for calling their own fouls and resolving disputes. Students may be required to run warm-ups or drills for teammates demonstrating knowledge acquired during prior Physical Education courses.

Skills in Math is a class that helps students feel more confident and get better at math. In this class, students practice important basics like addition, subtraction, fractions, and geometry, which help them in other math classes. Students also learn everyday math skills they can use in real life, like math for shopping, measuring, or budgeting. The class includes activities, step-by-step practice, and real-life examples, and students get the support they need to learn at their own speed. The goal of the course is to help students grow, understand math better, and feel ready for future math classes. The student must be recommended by a teacher for this course.

Bridge to Math 1 is a preparatory course designed to support students as they build the skills and confidence needed for success in Math 1. Students engage in problem-solving activities that emphasize making sense of algebraic relationships, working with numbers and quantities, and representing ideas using tables, graphs, and equations. Students also strengthen collaboration, communication, and critical thinking skills as they explain their ideas and learn from others. Students will practice the following skills: algebraic expressions, integers, equations and functions, decimals, fractions, exponents, ratios, proportions, percents, area, and graphing.

Math 1 is a foundational high school course in which students develop algebraic reasoning while making connections across geometry, and statistics. Students work through rich problem-solving tasks that ask them to represent relationships using graphs, tables, equations, and words. Through exploration and discussion, students analyze patterns, compare solution strategies, and justify their thinking using mathematical language. The course emphasizes modeling real-world situations and interpreting data to make sense of quantitative information. Students regularly collaborate with peers, communicate their ideas clearly, and reflect on their problem-solving processes. Math 1 builds the skills and habits of mind needed for continued success in higher-level mathematics. Units of study include the following: Sequences, Linear & Exponential Functions, Equations, Inequalities & Systems, Geometric Transformations & Symmetry, and Modeling Data.

Math 2 builds on the concepts and problem-solving strategies developed in Math 1 as students deepen their understanding of algebra and geometry. Students explore relationships of quadratics, absolute value, piecewise functions and use multiple representations including graphs, tables, diagrams, and equations, to analyze and solve problems. Through investigations involving geometric reasoning, students examine similarity, right triangles, and spatial relationships to make sense of mathematical structure. The course emphasizes reasoning, justification, and strategic thinking as students tackle increasingly complex tasks. Students collaborate regularly, communicate their ideas clearly, and compare solution methods. Math 2 supports continued growth in mathematical confidence and prepares students for more advanced coursework.
courses.prerequisites: Math 1

courses.description: Geometry is a course where students analyze figures using diagrams, coordinate representations, and algebraic reasoning to solve meaningful problems. Through exploration and visual modeling, students examine similarity, congruence, and the properties of polygons and circles. The course emphasizes explaining and justifying reasoning, making connections between algebra and geometry, and applying ideas to real-world situations. Students collaborate, test conjectures, and refine their thinking through discussion and problem solving. Geometry develops spatial reasoning and logical thinking skills that support continued success in mathematics.
courses.prerequisites: Math 1

courses.description: Problem Solving is a course that helps students strengthen and apply mathematical skills across a range of content areas through rich, non-routine problems. Students engage in challenging tasks that require them to analyze situations, choose appropriate strategies, and reflect on the effectiveness of their approaches. The course emphasizes critical thinking, persistence, and making sense of unfamiliar problems rather than memorizing procedures. Students also practice test-taking strategies and learn how to approach SAT and ACT–style questions with confidence and efficiency. Through discussion and reflection, students refine their reasoning and communication skills. This course is recommended for juniors or seniors preparing for SAT or ACT assessments.
courses.prerequisites: Math 2

courses.description: Math 3 builds on the mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies developed in Math 1 and Math 2 as students engage with more complex and connected ideas. Students explore relationships between functions, analyze patterns, and use algebraic, geometric, and trigonometric reasoning to model and solve problems. Through investigations and real-world applications, students make connections across representations such as graphs, equations, diagrams, and data. The course emphasizes explaining thinking, justifying solutions, and evaluating the reasonableness of results. Students collaborate regularly and communicate their ideas clearly as they tackle challenging tasks. Math 3 prepares students for advanced mathematical study by strengthening both conceptual understanding and strategic problem solving. Units of study in Math 3 include the following: Inverse Functions, Logarithms, Polynomials, Modeling with Geometry, and Trigonometry.
courses.prerequisites: Math 2

courses.description: Advanced Mathematical Topics is an exploratory course in which students investigate a variety of advanced mathematical ideas through problem solving, modeling, and analysis. Students work with abstract and applied concepts to analyze patterns, represent relationships, and solve complex problems using multiple representations. The course encourages curiosity, persistence, and creative thinking as students explore less traditional areas of mathematics and make connections across topics. Technology, including graphing calculators, is used to visualize relationships and support mathematical reasoning. Students regularly explain their thinking, compare strategies, and refine their understanding through discussion and reflection. Advanced Mathematical Topics will examine the following math topics including: Combinatorics & Probability, Sequences & Series, Conics, and Polar Coordinates & Complex #’s. This course is appropriate for students who have completed Math 3 or higher-level math and are interested in deepening their mathematical experience.
courses.prerequisites: Math 3

courses.description: Pre-Calculus examines all math topics at a deeper level with a strong emphasis on using real-world Pre-Calculus is a course in which students deepen and connect their understanding of algebraic and trigonometric ideas in preparation for advanced mathematics. Students analyze functions, explore relationships between multiple representations, and use mathematical models to investigate real-world situations. Through problem solving and guided exploration, students strengthen their ability to reason abstractly, make connections across topics, and explain their thinking clearly. Technology, including graphing calculators, is used to visualize behavior of functions and support analysis. The course emphasizes persistence, strategic thinking, and collaboration as students tackle increasingly complex problems. The topics included in this course are linear relations and functions, systems of linear equations and inequalities, polynomial and rational functions, trigonometric functions, identities and equations, exponential and logarithmic functions. *Pre-Calculus prepares students for college-level mathematics and may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met.
courses.prerequisites: Math 3
courses.notes: Footnote *: may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met

courses.description: Statistics is a course for students interested in understanding how data is collected, analyzed, and used to draw meaningful conclusions. Students analyze real-world data and situations, and interpret results using numerical, graphical, and written representations. Students will design a semester-long investigative project based on the core concepts of the course. The course emphasizes statistical reasoning, critical reading, and clear written communication as students evaluate claims and justify conclusions with evidence. Students regularly use technology, including graphing calculators, to model data and support analysis. Through discussion and reflection, students build skills that are valuable in research-based fields and everyday decision making. *This course prepares students for college-level statistics and may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met.
courses.prerequisites: Math 2
courses.notes: Footnote *: may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met

courses.description: Calculus is a one-semester course taught in conjunction with AP Calculus, covering the first-semester topics in the sequence. Students explore limits, continuity, and the concepts of derivatives, derivatives of functions, real-world applications of derivatives, and integrals. Technology, including graphing calculators, is used to visualize and deepen understanding. The course emphasizes explaining reasoning, justifying solutions, and connecting ideas across mathematical topics.
courses.prerequisites: Pre-Calculus

courses.description: AP Calculus 1 (AB) is a college-level course designed for students ready to explore the fundamental ideas of calculus in depth. Students investigate limits, continuity, derivatives, and integrals through problem solving, and real-world applications. They learn to analyze functions, solve complex problems, and interpret results while justifying their reasoning using mathematical language. Students also develop strategies for approaching challenging tasks independently and collaboratively. AP Calculus 1 (AB) prepares students for success in AP exams and for future studies in science, mathematics, engineering, and other advanced fields.
courses.prerequisites: Pre-Calculus and Summer assignments are required.

courses.description: This course will focus on drama as a unique form of creative expression. A workshop approach will be used to increase students’ comfort with playwriting and acting. Students will work on their acting through established plays, acting games, and their own writing.

Students experience the process of learning a wide variety of band literature in varying musical styles. The ensemble performs in several concerts and parades. Students experience the process of improving technique, rhythm reading and sight reading in order to become more independent. Students have the opportunity to receive critical feedback on their individual performance as well as critique and reflect on their personal and their ensemble’s process and growth. Students are expected to participate in all performances which often occur in the evenings or on weekends.
courses.prerequisites: Minimum two years of band experience or permission of the director.
courses.notes: Offered During Compass

courses.description: Students experience the process of learning a wide variety of choral literature in varying musical styles and languages including sacred and seasonal music. The ensemble performs in several concerts. Students experience the process of improving vocal technique, rhythm reading and sight singing in order to become more independent. Students receive critical feedback on their individual performance and critique and reflect on their personal and their ensemble’s process and growth. Students are expected to participate in all performances which often occur in the evenings or on weekends.
courses.notes: Offered During Compass

courses.description: This class provides introductory guitar lessons to students in a group setting. No prior experience is needed. Students experience the process of learning to tune guitar strings, change guitar strings and the fundamentals of guitar technique in order to perform during the semester. Students follow a guitar method book with different styles of music and accompaniment patterns. VUHS guitars are available for use, but students are encouraged to bring their own.

Students learn secondary instruments while continuing to experience growth on their primary instruments. They compose and arrange music designed to be played by small ensembles. Students experience the process of working toward a performance and reflect on their process and personal growth.
courses.prerequisites: High School Symphonic Band

courses.description: This course is designed to give students an understanding of the history of modern music and the ability to listen to music in an active and professional way. This course is designed for all students, including those who have little to no previous music experience. Music is presented with a historical perspective and emphasizes prominent composers, musical periods and styles. Students will get to learn about the origins of our current music, the development of electronic music and everything in between.

Students will learn the basics of how music really works and will be provided with the tools to write their own music. Students will study chords, melody, harmony, rhythm, counterpoint and part writing to understand, analyze and compose written music. In addition, students will get practice in ear training to better understand the music they listen to and recognize what is happening in both modern songs and classical compositions.

This class is designed to provide introductory piano lessons to students in a group setting. No prior experience is needed. Students experience the process of learning the fundamentals of piano technique in order to perform during the semester. They have the opportunity to create a short composition and reflect on their growth during the semester.
This class is a continuation of Piano Class I. Students further refine their piano technique and create a more advanced composition.
courses.prerequisites: Piano Class I

courses.description: This class is an exploration into production and creation of popular music through the medium of modern “rock” band for students in grades 9-12. Students will be provided with the opportunity to learn and grow in basic knowledge of guitar, keyboard, bass, drum set, vocals, and creation of music through a “rock” combo. This course is designed so that any level of student can be a part of the ensemble and directed towards growth on each of the instruments. (Students wishing to play instruments not listed above are still welcome to join.)

This course is designed for students who wish to improve their vocal technique and solo voice. They explore aspects of good posture, diction, breathing, and tone as well as study solo repertoire in classical, pop, and musical theater styles. Students have in-class coaching and performance opportunities and study sight-singing.
courses.prerequisites: One year of Concert Choir or teacher permission

courses.description: This class provides an introduction to music from around the world through drumming. Students will have the opportunity to play with the Vergennes African Drum Ensemble and learn the fundamentals of drumming on a number of different percussion instruments. Students will also learn the basics of reading music and the historical context for the music we perform.

courses.course_name: Introduction to Life and Physical Science
courses.description: This is a standards-based course focusing on creating scientifically literate students. Students will learn about topics in both physical and life science, basic laboratory skills, and other skills necessary to be successful in the science classroom. Topics range from the origin of our universe to cellular energetics. Ultimately students will gain a better understanding of the science they experience in their everyday lives and to help inform their future course selections. The majority of class assignments can be completed during class. Generally, outside work will only be required when students do not use class time effectively. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Systems, Energy, and Matter.
courses.notes: Foundational course that supports access to future coursework, recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

courses.course_name: Biology: Anatomy and Physiology (formerly Human Biology)
courses.description: This science course starts with cell structures and functions. Students will build microscope skills in order to identify cells and organelles. We will study each body system and focus on how healthy systems maintain homeostasis, while disruptions in homeostasis cause illness. Within each unit students will have freedom to explore diseases, build models, and practice lab techniques. Life is going to throw students “curveballs”; they or someone they love has been diagnosed with a disease and now students must learn about it and make a plan for supporting this person. This class requires use of class time and some time at home to finish assignments. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Systems, and Structure and Function.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

courses.description: This course will explore ecosystems, including photosynthetic producers, food webs, invasive species, ecosystem dynamics, and biomes. Students will delve into key characteristics of living things, as well as specific traits of the diverse animal groups through reading, exploring local natural resources, and hands-on simulations. There are several choice-based projects for students to learn about topics of interest to them. This course emphasizes class work rather than homework, but work will need to be finished at home if class time isn’t used effectively. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Change Over Time, Stewardship, Energy, and Systems.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

courses.description: This new course will offer students an opportunity to explore how DNA works. We will explore the fundamental principles of how inherited traits are passed down (genetics) and how these traits change over time in populations (evolution), as well as how scientists can manipulate DNA to alter both genetics and the course of natural selection. Key topics include the structure and function of DNA, protein synthesis, inheritance patterns, genetic variation, natural selection, and how these mechanisms drive speciation and other evolutionary processes. This course will require students to spend some time outside of class to finish assignments. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Systems, Structure and Function, and Change over Time.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

courses.description: This course provides students with the opportunity to explore the important systems and processes that shape our planet, influence our lives, and inform environmental decision making. Major content knowledge will center around understanding the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere as systems. Application of that content knowledge will be integrated into experiences with environmental stewardship. These experiences will include outside projects working with local invasive species, restoration ecology, and environmental testing. Workload emphasizes completion during class by fully engaged students and may involve finishing classwork, making outdoor observations, and collecting samples as homework. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will include Systems and Patterns, and Stewardship.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

courses.description: This class will cover topics in physics with an emphasis on establishing a strong conceptual understanding of content and basic math foundation. Application of content is embedded in connections made through hands-on experiences related to daily life and careers. Main topics will include motion, force, energy, waves, and electricity. Workload emphasizes completion during class by fully engaged students and will involve finishing as homework. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will be Change Over Time, Matter and Energy, and Systems and Patterns.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

courses.description: This class will introduce students to the fundamental content and skills related to the field of chemistry by emphasizing the establishment of a strong conceptual understanding and basic math foundations. Application of content is embedded in connections made through hands-on experiences related to daily life and careers. Main topics will include properties of matter and its behavior during changes. Workload emphasizes completion during class by fully engaged students and will involve finishing as homework. The VUHS Science Proficiency covered is Matter and Energy.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

courses.description: This laboratory science course is designed as a foundation for students interested in the future study of chemistry, a STEM profession, or medical profession. The first half of the course focuses on concepts concerning the classification of matter, atomic structure, and chemical bonding. The second half investigates increasingly specific conceptual and mathematical aspects of chemical behavior and chemical reactions. Laboratory work is an integral and frequent part of the course where students gain laboratory skills while experiencing hands-on connections to content. Routine homework will be expected as preparation for and extension of the classroom experience. The VUHS Science Proficiency covered is Matter and Energy.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and successful completion of Math 2

courses.description: This laboratory science course is intended for students that have a strong interest and aptitude for future study and/or application of science in STEM fields. The scope of topics will be those of a traditional physics course focusing on mechanics, waves, optics, electricity, and magnetism. An emphasis is placed on developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills through the application of mathematical and conceptual understanding of content. Labs and projects are inquiry based and allow students to discover fundamental relationships that govern the world around them. Routine homework will be expected as preparation for and extension of the classroom experience. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will be Change Over Time, Matter and Energy, and Systems and Patterns.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and successful completion of Math 3, or concurrent enrollment in Math 3 with a math teacher recommendation

courses.description: This is a college-level laboratory course based on the Advanced Placement Biology curriculum. The course covers a wide variety of biology topics in great detail and thus will make demands of even the most dedicated students. Topics range from biochemistry, cells and genetics in the first semester, to evolution and ecology in the second semester. Summer work is meant to review basic chemistry content and give students a better understanding of the work level before the add/drop period. In addition to reading a college-level text, students will demonstrate understanding through a variety of written assignments, perform inquiry-based laboratory experiments, and prepare to take the AP test in May. Students should expect to commit a significant amount of time to this course’s workload. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Structure and Function, Systems, Energy, Matter, Change Over Time, and Stewardship.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and either Wildlife Ecology; Introduction to Anatomy and Physiology; Genetics, Evolution, and Biotechnology; or Chemistry. Ms. Thompson’s signature on the course selection sheet is required. Summer assignments required.

courses.description: This is a laboratory course based on the College Board AP Physics 1 curriculum. To be successful in this course, students must understand basic principles of physics, and demonstrate knowledge using critical thinking and reasoning skills. Key components of demonstration will be the ability to express thoughts mathematically, and conceptually through written language and calculation. Students need to be academically motivated, have a strong foundation in math, and have an interest in developing problem-solving skills. The course covers the full breadth of classical physics topics found in a first semester introductory algebra/trig-based college physics course. Consequently, students should expect to devote a significant amount of time studying material beyond the designated class time. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will be Change Over Time, Matter and Energy, and Systems and Patterns.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and successful completion of, or concurrent enrollment in, Pre-Calculus. Mr. Francis’ signature is required on the course selection sheet. Summer assignments required.

courses.description: The human world around us is constantly changing. In World Geography and Cultures we are going to investigate the factors that have influenced change throughout the course of human history. We are going to begin our studies by being able to identify countries from many different continents, investigating world religions, and learning about how beliefs and values shape cultures. We will study concepts such as culture, civilizations, philosophy, nationalism, imperialism, and genocide. As we look at all of these larger pieces of the puzzle of world history we will look at how groups of people and individuals make change. Throughout this course, we will work on our analytical skills, by learning how to gather reliable sources, find accurate pieces of evidence and make solid claims. These skills will allow us to understand our world better and allow us to go out and become better world citizens.
courses.notes: Foundational course that supports access to future coursework, recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

courses.description: Students focus on the major forces that contributed to the shaping and emergence of modern America and make connections to their own lives at the local, state, national and international levels. Students use historical inquiry methods to conduct research. They will understand the value of consulting both primary and secondary sources to help them gain an understanding of the history of the United States. Students use current technology to conduct and present their research.
courses.notes: Recommended for 10th grade

courses.description: In this century, it is critically important to not only be a citizen of one’s own nation, but to see the world as a global community. In this course students explore how the American identity and experience has been shaped—and will continue to be shaped—by a diverse array of cultural influences and traditions. Students compare and contrast social and political movements while investigating contemporary issues. Students look at how these issues impact local, state, national and global policies and laws. This class includes critical analysis of public issues and allows students to participate in research, discussion, debate and real-world experiences supporting the curriculum.
courses.prerequisites: U.S. History

courses.description: This class provides students with the opportunity to better understand the world. Students will stay up to date on current issues via class discussion, research, and presentations. They will learn critical thinking skills, how to evaluate media bias, and how to discuss difficult topics respectfully. Students will be challenged to strengthen their opinions with evidence and explore multiple perspectives on a variety of issues.

This course introduces the scientific study of the human mind and behavior. Understanding the hidden drivers of human nature, from how we learn to how we handle stress, allows us to navigate our lives and relationships with greater empathy and insight. We will explore three major units: positive psychology, memory/learning, and social influence. You will participate in “psych-labs” to test theories of perception and analyze case studies of famous experiments. By the end of the term, you will be able to identify cognitive biases and interpret scientific research. Expect a mix of collaborative projects and multiple-choice assessments. While there is no heavy nightly racing, you will engage in daily experiments, film analysis, and classroom discussions. Some project work may require time outside of class. This is for anyone curious about people or considering careers in counseling, marketing, or healthcare. No prior science background is required. Just an open mind and a willingness to look at the world through a different lens.

Vermont History will provide students with learning opportunities to analyze and discuss the impact of major forces that contributed to the shaping of Vermont from the early geological era to the present. We will use primary and secondary sources to learn about our local community and the history of Vermont. Students will conduct research about local, historical topics and present their findings by writing small papers, and making maps and timelines. This course will help students understand how geography and historical impacts have impacted the state they now live in.

AP Government and Politics offers students an in-depth exploration of the American political system, emphasizing the foundations, institutions, policies, and processes that shape the U.S. government. This course covers the Constitution, federalism, civil liberties, political ideologies, interest groups, political parties, and the roles of the three branches of government. Students will analyze how citizens engage with the government through voting, activism, and public opinion. The course also highlights the impact of media and political behavior on policy-making. Through critical reading, discussion, and writing, students develop the skills needed to evaluate government actions and political developments. By preparing for the AP exam, students gain a comprehensive understanding of the political landscape, fostering informed citizenship and encouraging active participation in democratic processes.
courses.prerequisites: Requires Social Studies teacher signature on course request sheet.
courses.fulfills_text: Successful completion of this course fulfills the Modern Citizenship requirement

courses.description: This course addresses the belief that now is the time for students to discover if any aspects of Engineering or Architecture could be part of their future. It presents the idea that know-how is not necessarily an intuitive ability. Students can begin to develop an operational knowledge of Engineering and Architecture by applying themselves to a disciplined course syllabus. While learning 3D software will expand students’ capacity to professionally present work, they must also bring a free expression of imagination and creativity to fully realize the opportunity this curriculum presents. Those who discover an interest in these fields are encouraged to enroll in the PHCC Engineering & Architecture Design Program during grades 11 or 12.

This course expands upon the concept that Engineering and Architecture precepts are a conveyable body of knowledge. Those who wish to further develop their understanding from CAD I will complete relevant assignments focusing on innovative design and systems analysis incorporating science, technology, engineering & math. This curriculum requires each student to propose, complete and present several Product Design Innovations. Students can continue to pursue their interest in these fields by enrolling in the Engineering & Architecture Design program at PAHCC.

This course is designed for students who have completed CAD I and CAD II and wish to progress and practice their skills on individual, self-directed projects. Students will further explore the advanced tools in the Key Creator, Chief Architect, and 3D printing software. Students may also choose to explore and learn introductory skills in other CAD software such as SketchUp, Revit, and AutoCAD360. Students must have excellent foundational CAD skills, and be self-motivated to create an individual path to progress their learning.

Equip yourself with the essential tools to thrive in a digital world. This course focuses on mastering everyday apps like the Google Suite while navigating the complexities of ethical AI use. Students gain troubleshooting skills to fix common tech issues and explore digital literacy. Additionally, students have the opportunity to apply design skills to create tangible products using tools like vinyl cutters and a glowforge lasercutter. Students leave with a versatile toolkit of practical digital skills for future success.

This course introduces the fundamentals of logic and design using LEGO Spike Prime kits. Students combine hands-on building with computer science, constructing mechanical attachments with LEGO Technic pieces to solve specific puzzles. You will explore modern problem-solving techniques, including an introduction to AI-assisted coding, to program robots to operate autonomously. The focus is on critical thinking, troubleshooting, and teamwork. This is a beginner-level course designed to build a foundation in computational thinking through trial and error.

Ever thought of starting your own business or being involved in the management of a small business? In this course students choose a reasonable business concept and write a real business plan detailing what it would look like to put their ideas into action. The business plan must clearly explain how the business will operate, the target market, and the financial situation. Students consider what technology can make this task easier or the final product better. The class visits with local business owners during the course. Students should be able to impress an admissions counselor, a potential employer, or even a lender with their completed business plan.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is eligible to earn .5 Technology credit and .5 elective credit, or 1.0 elective credit. Please consult your school counselor for details.

courses.description: In this course, students explore and complete various activities, challenges and projects based on STEM (Science Technology Engineering Math). STEM proficient students are able to answer complex questions and develop solutions for challenges and real-world problems while applying the rigor and relevance of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics content. The challenges are “hands-on” activities intended to develop and reinforce critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

Art Essentials is an introductory art course for students to learn the basics of two dimensional art. It is a prerequisite for every other high school art offering. In Art Essentials students will explore and experiment with a variety of artistic media and techniques as they study the elements of art (line, shape, value, space, texture, color and form). Each unit of study will focus on a different element of art through a variety of formative assignments with a final summative project highlighting students’ knowledge/skill in that element in a finished work of art for display. The majority of work will be done in class, but there will be biweekly sketchbook formative assignments for students to work on independently outside of class. All students who wish to take visual art should take Art Essentials as a starting point.

and dive deeper into painting. In this course students will expand on their basic drawing skills learned in Art Essentials. Students will improve their skills in observational drawing, shading, painting, color theory, and composition through still life drawing and portrait painting from a combination of life and photographs. Students will work with a variety of drawing and painting media, including but not limited to graphite, charcoal, colored pencils, and acrylic paint. The majority of work will be done in class, but there will be biweekly sketchbook formative assignments for students to work on independently outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Essentials
courses.notes: Intermediate Drawing & Painting is an opportunity for students to push their technical drawing skills

courses.description: Advanced Painting & Color Theory is designed for students looking to challenge themselves in painting and gain a more intimate knowledge and understanding of color. In this course students will learn advanced acrylic painting techniques. The majority of work will be done in class.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Essentials and Intermediate Drawing & Painting

courses.description: This course offers students an excellent opportunity to grow as an artist while developing within a medium that increases technical proficiency. In this course students will explore forms of artistic digital media including digital illustration and stop motion animation on iPads. Class time will be spent learning the basics of digital illustration with Procreate, working on various assignments and learning how to incorporate layers, levels, and other editing tools into a wide variety of images and themes. Students will be introduced to the iMovie program while creating animated short videos.
courses.prerequisites: Art Essentials

courses.description: In this course, students will expand on the skills learned in Digital Media. Students will extend their learning in digital illustration, graphic design, and animation using a variety of creative programs to create more advanced and in depth, independent artistic projects. The majority of the work will be done in class once students have designed independent projects to work on and complete during the semester. This course is for students who have taken Digital Media and are looking for a new creative challenge
courses.prerequisites: Digital Media

courses.description: In this course students will create multiple types of additive sculpture with a variety of materials. They will explore 3-D design and learn how to build sculptures of humans, animals, buildings, and more. The work will all be done in class through design creation, review with the teacher through conversation, and the final build of the sculpture. This class is for students who have taken Art Essentials and would like to expand their artistic knowledge in 3-dimensional design.
courses.prerequisites: Art Essentials

courses.description: In this course students will have the opportunity to extend their learning from Sculpture . Each project will build off of the skills they gained in Sculpture and challenge them to build new skills. This course is designed for students who have a strong interest in sculpture making and are looking for a challenge. Students will have the opportunity to build larger scale figurative sculptures and larger sculpture installations.
courses.prerequisites: Sculpture

courses.description: AP Studio Art is a conglomerate of three AP courses: AP Drawing, AP 2-D Design, and AP 3-D Design. Each of these courses are designed to be equivalent to an introductory college-level studio art course. Students will choose which of these three courses they wish to pursue based on their own personal artistic strengths and interests. Students will refine and apply skills and ideas they develop throughout the course to produce a cohesive body of creative work exploring common themes and media in depth. AP Studio Art courses culminate in a portfolio submission to the College Board in the spring.
courses.prerequisites: Art teacher signature on course request sheet. Successful completion of Art Essentials and at least one additional art course. The course is open to Juniors and Seniors only.

courses.description: Students begin developing novice-level proficiency in the target language. By the end of Level 1, students can understand and use basic words, phrases, and short sentences related to everyday topics such as family, school, hobbies, and personal preferences. Instruction emphasizes pronunciation, sound patterns, and foundational grammatical structures to support accurate communication. Students also begin developing cultural awareness through exploration of customs and perspectives in regions where the language is spoken.

Students communicate about an expanded set of familiar topics such as daily life, food, travel, and descriptions of physical and emotional states, while developing greater control of basic grammatical structures. Cultural understanding is deepened through continued exploration of customs and perspectives in regions where the language is spoken.

Students express and support opinions, analyze ideas, and make cultural and historical connections using the target language. The course emphasizes real-world communication, critical thinking, and a deeper understanding of cultural perspectives in regions where the language is spoken.

By the end of the course, students can understand and express ideas in extended spoken and written language, including multiple-paragraph writing. Students narrate, describe, explain, and support opinions while engaging with topics such as society, education, science, politics, and the arts. They participate in sustained conversations and comprehend longer spoken and written texts, including authentic materials. The course emphasizes advanced communication skills, cultural understanding, and real-world language use.

courses.description: Conversational German is a highly participatory course designed to strengthen students’ interpersonal communication skills in the target language. Students engage in sustained listening and speaking practice through discussions, storytelling, role-play, and collaborative activities. Emphasis is placed on maintaining conversations with greater confidence, flexibility, and depth, including the ability to discuss both everyday situations and more abstract topics. Vocabulary and language structures are expanded as needed to support spontaneous communication. Topics vary based on student interest. Consistent use of German is expected throughout the course.
courses.prerequisites: German III or German IV; students who have only completed German II with strong speaking skills can take this course with instructor permission

courses.description: Dual Enrollment allows eligible students to earn both high school and college credit through approved college courses. Dual enrollment is one of several ways students may access college-level learning while enrolled at VUHS and is subject to a required planning and approval process. Students must have completed their sophomore year and receive prior approval from the School Counseling Office before enrolling in a dual enrollment course, whether using a state funded voucher or paying independently. Approval is based on readiness for college level coursework, progress toward graduation requirements, and the student’s overall academic plan. Dual enrollment is not automatic and cannot be arranged independently. Approved dual enrollment courses become part of both the VUHS high school transcript and the college transcript. Dual enrollment plans must be reflected in the student’s Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) as part of the graduation planning process. VUHS students most commonly participate in dual enrollment through the following Vermont institutions: ●University of Vermont ●Vermont State University ●Community College of Vermont ●Norwich University ●Saint Michael’s College ●Champlain College Availability, timelines, and course options vary by institution and by year. Students interested in dual enrollment should meet with their school counselor early in the planning process to review eligibility, required steps, and approved course options.
courses.notes: program; grade levels derived from 'Students must have completed their sophomore year'

courses.description: Vermont’s Early College Program is a full-year alternative to a student’s senior year of high school. Through this program, students complete their senior year of high school while earning some or all of their first year of college credits at the same time. College tuition is covered by the state of Vermont. Some Early College programs offer on-campus housing. Families and students are responsible for costs not covered by the state, including housing (if applicable), transportation, textbooks, and meals. Early College programs are available through the Community College of Vermont, Norwich University, and Vermont State University. Early College participation requires planning and school approval. Interested students should connect with their school counselor for guidance, eligibility review, and support with the application process.
courses.provider: Community College of Vermont, Norwich University, Vermont State University
courses.notes: program; grade level derived from 'full-year alternative to a student's senior year'

courses.description: Eligible seniors may apply to take a Middlebury College course at no cost. Enrollment is limited, and the timing of a Middlebury course may impact a student’s Vergennes Union High School schedule. To qualify, students must be prepared for college-level work, have successfully completed the highest-level coursework available at VUHS in the subject area they wish to study, and meet additional Middlebury College requirements. A three- or four-credit Middlebury College course counts as one credit toward high school graduation. Students do not earn college credit from Middlebury College, and the course does not transfer to other colleges or universities. Students interested in this option must meet with their school counselor for information about eligibility, additional requirements, and the application process. Applications are submitted in the spring of junior year for semester one courses and in December of senior year for semester two courses.
courses.credits_text: A three- or four-credit Middlebury College course counts as one credit toward high school graduation
courses.notes: program; grade level derived from 'Eligible seniors'; credits derived from the stated 3- or 4-credit equivalence

courses.description: The Walden Year is an outdoor education program offered through The Willowell Foundation. Launched in fall 2024, the program acknowledges the history of The Walden Project, an outdoor learning program previously offered through Vergennes Union High School, and operates as a distinct and separate program. The Walden Year provides an interdisciplinary, immersive learning experience with a focus on environmental studies, writing, and philosophy. Inspired by Henry David Thoreau’s time at Walden Pond, the program emphasizes learning through sustained engagement with the natural world and supports student-centered, inquiry-based learning connected to individual interests and reflection. Students interested in The Walden Year should indicate this option on their Course Request sheet. Doing so will prompt a meeting with a school counselor to determine whether this flexible pathway aligns with graduation requirements, learning goals, and individual needs. If the pathway is determined to be an appropriate fit, the school will support the student in making a connection with the program.
courses.notes: program; operated by The Willowell Foundation, distinct from VUHS
